segments.text: Meet the world's tiniest pencil. No lead, just electrons. A classic analog oscilloscope turns a
changing voltage into a line of light. Inside its glass tube is an electron gun. A little assembly
that releases, controls, accelerates and focuses electrons. Let's follow them. First, the heater.
In this common design a small filament warms a separate coated cathode. This is an indirectly
heated cathode. The heater supplies warmth. The cathode supplies the beam's electrons.
electrons. Heat gives some electrons enough energy to escape the surface, a process called
thermionic emission. They were already in the material. We have not invented new electrons.
Electrons arriving through the cathode's electrical connection replace those carried
away by the beam. Meanwhile the tube's vacuum removes nearly all the gas, allowing electrons
to travel with very few collisions. Immediately ahead sits the control grid, usually a small
metal cup with an opening. It is held negative relative to the cathode. Its electric field
restricts how many electrons can enter the beam, make it less negative, and more pass
through – a brighter trace. Make it more negative, and the beam dwindles. A cut-off
it is stopped. Nothing has to slide shut. This electrical gate can blank the beam between
sweeps, a remarkably punctual doorman. Next, accelerating electrodes, called V nodes, establish
voltages more positive than the cathode. Their electric fields give the electrons
forward speed as they pass through aligned openings. Positive here means relative to the
cathode, not necessarily positive relative to ground. The power supply provides this energy.
The heater releases electrons from the surface. These voltage differences do the accelerating.
Speed alone would give us a rather untidy splodge. Shaped electrodes at carefully chosen voltages
create an electrostatic lens. Its curved electric field bends the paths of electrons towards a small
optical lens brings light to a focus. There is no piece of glass in this lens. Turn the
focus control and you adjust its electrical strength.
Now the beam reaches two pairs of deflection plates arranged at right angles. Because electrons
carry negative charge, they bend towards the more positive plate. One pair steers vertically,
the other horizontally. The input signal, suitably amplified, drives the vertical pair.
As that voltage rises and falls, the spot follows it up and down. To spread that
movement across time, a ramp voltage sweeps the spot steadily from left to right.
During the rapid return called flyback, the beam is blanked. At the screen, energetic electrons
excite a phosphor coating, which emits light and briefly continues glowing.
The travelling spot and its fading trail make the waveform. Our drawn beam path is an illustration.
The light appears at the screen. Finally, the trigger waits for a chosen event, such
as the signal crossing a selected voltage in the rising direction. Each sweep then begins
at the same point in a repeating signal, so the trace settles. Height tells us voltage,
distance across tells us time, an electron gun, some careful steering and rather lovely
handwriting.
